papers.title_in_file: Interaction graph connectivity - Quantum Computing Inc
papers.what_it_is: A Quantum Computing Inc web lesson arguing that full interaction-graph connectivity matters for optimization hardware, using treewidth to bound how large a fully connected problem a quasi-planar chip can embed.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because light moves and light pulses can easily be divided into parts, realizing full connectivity in optical devices is conceptually straightforward.
quotes: since light is constantly moving and light pulses can easily be divided into parts, realizing full connectivity is conceptually straightforward.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of the connectivity of optical devices; the lesson cites the literature rather than proving it.

assertions.value: The authors describe a coupling scheme in which a small part of one light pulse is pulled off and added to another pulse, and they point to a 2016 paper's figure 1 as an example.
quotes: An effective scheme can be to simply pull off a small part of one pulse and add it to another (see figure 1 of this paper from 2016 for example).
assertions.certainty_reason: A scheme attributed to other work; the lesson does not test it.

assertions.value: The authors state that interactions can also be simulated by classical feedback (measuring, then using a laser to return the feedback pulse), that this approach disrupts entanglement, and that it gives an easy way to experiment with large-scale highly-connected devices.
quotes: The interactions can also be simulated using classical feedback, by measuring and using a laser to return what the feedback pulse should be.
Although such an approach disrupts entanglement, it provides an easy way to experiment with large-scale highly-connected devices.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the limit (entanglement is disrupted) in its own description of the feedback approach.

assertions.value: The authors claim that most, if not all, real industrial optimization problems have highly connected interactivity graphs, and that the overhead of mapping them to less-connected hardware can be huge.
quotes: Most, if not all, real industrial optimization problems have highly connected interactivity graphs, and the overhead of mapping to less-connected hardware can be huge
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim with no evidence given in the lesson.
assertions.reader_inference: No survey or citation is given for the 'most, if not all' statement.

assertions.value: The authors report a back-of-the-envelope estimate that, under realistic constraints, a highly connected problem with a few hundred variables takes on the order of 10,000 qubits on a non-fully-connected chip architecture, and that a typical 10,000 variable problem would need on the order of 100 million physical qubits.
quotes: a highly connected problem with a few hundred variables (still small in terms of optimization problems), will take on the order of 10,000 qubits to map.
More typical 10,000 variable problems would require the order of 100 million physical qubits to map.
assertions.certainty_reason: A rough estimate the authors call a quick back-of-the-envelope calculation; its inputs (the TRIAD-based qubit estimate with d=6 and d=20) are only shown in a figure.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer does not carry the figure that shows the estimate for d=6 and d=20, so the figures cannot be checked from the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that on their hardware one qubit is one variable of an optimization problem, because any qubit or qudit can interact with any other, so a binary variable maps to a single qubit and a discrete variable maps to a single qudit.
quotes: Our hardware does not have this issue, one qubit is one variable in an optimization problem.
A single binary variable maps to a single qubit, and a single discrete variable maps to a single qudit.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of its own product.

assertions.value: The authors state that if interactions are restricted and a problem is not naturally compatible with the restrictions, the only way to solve it is a one-to-many mapping, in which each variable is mapped to many qubits or qudits.
quotes: then the only way to do it is through a one-to-many mapping, where each variable is mapped to many qubits or qudit.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim stated without proof at this point; the treewidth section gives the supporting argument.

assertions.value: The authors state, as the headline result, that for realistic restrictions from placement on a two-dimensional chip the size of a highly-connected problem that can be solved goes as the square root of the size of the device, whereas on their hardware it scales directly as the size.
quotes: The headline result here is that for realistic restrictions from placement on a two-dimensional chip, the size of a highly-connected problem that can be solved goes as the square root of the size of the device, whereas on our hardware it scales directly as the size.
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson argues it by a sketch of a tree decomposition that is not a formal proof, and it rests on the unproved treewidth monotonicity claim; the hardware half is a vendor statement.
assertions.reader_inference: The scaling argument is informal. It assumes an interaction range much smaller than the graph size, a condition the lesson states only in the treewidth section.

assertions.value: The authors examine the TRIAD method, proposed in a cited paper, for mapping a complete interaction graph to quasi-planar hardware, using as examples d=6 and d=20, where d is the number of qubits each qubit can interact with, and they note the estimate is not necessarily accurate when n is close to d.
quotes: we examine the TRIAD method to map a complete interaction graph to quasi-planar hardware proposed in this paper
in this example we consider as examples d=6 and d=20
note that this estimate is not necessarily accurate when n
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the setup and the caveat of its own example in this passage.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer garbles the closing math of the caveat (a repeated 'n' and 'd' form), so the quote stops before the approximation sign.

assertions.value: The authors define the interactivity graph as the graph of what can directly interact with what, and say that on their analog hardware any qubit or qudit can be made to interact with any other, so the graph is a complete graph.
quotes: we can think of an interactivity graph, which is the graph of what can directly interact with what, as a graph with edges joining all of the nodes
any qubit or qudit can be made to interact with any other one.
assertions.certainty_reason: The definition is general, but the full connectivity of the vendor's analog hardware is a vendor statement.

assertions.value: The authors state that in superconducting circuits each variable often corresponds to a physical circuit element with a size constraint, and coupler circuits can only be so long, so the interaction graph cannot be fully connected and is instead quasi-planar, in which a node can interact only with nodes nearby in a 2D plane.
quotes: the interaction graph for such devices cannot be fully connected, it must instead be a type of graph we call quasi-planar
In a quasi-planar graph nodes (representing the qubits), can only have edges (be allowed to interact) with others which are nearby in a 2D plane.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines quasi-planar in this passage; the application to superconducting circuits is the paper's stated scope.
assertions.reader_inference: The lesson applies the quasi-planar model to superconducting circuits as a whole; it does not discuss devices with longer-range couplers.

assertions.value: The authors state that the interaction graph of a problem is read from its QUBO (or QUDO) representation by assigning a node to each variable and an edge whenever there is a non-zero off-diagonal element in the QUBO matrix.
assertions.anchor: Interaction graphs of optimization problems, paragraph 1
quotes: We can assign a node to each variable, and then assign edges between them whenever there is a non-zero off-diagonal element in the QUBO matrix.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the construction in this passage.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the conventional traveling salesperson formulation, with a variable for each city at each tour position, the city-once and one-city-at-a-time constraints and the distance penalties make the interaction graph highly connected, though not quite fully connected.
assertions.anchor: Interaction graphs of optimization problems, paragraph 3
quotes: While not quite fully connected, it is clear that the interaction graph representing a traveling salesperson problem is highly connected.
assertions.certainty_reason: An argued claim with no count of edges or measured example.

assertions.value: The authors state that the most used method to map a more connected graph to a less connected one is minor embedding, in which connected groups of qubits (graph minors) are strongly coupled together so they act as a single variable, and that it is not the only method.
assertions.anchor: Mapping to a less connected graph
quotes: The most used method is one called minor embedding , where connected groups of qubits ("graph minors" in technical terms) are strongly coupled together so they act as a single variable.
Technically minor embedding isn't the only way to map a more connected graph to a less connected one
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines minor embedding as it uses the term.

assertions.value: The authors state the rules of a tree decomposition: nodes connected by an edge in the original graph must appear together in some node of the new graph, all new-graph nodes holding the same original node must be connected, the new graph must be a tree with no loops, and the goal is to minimize the number of original nodes in the largest new node.
assertions.anchor: Graph theory: treewidth and tree decompositions, paragraph 2
quotes: Any nodes connected by edges in the original graph must appear in the same node at least once in the new graph
The new graph must be a tree, it cannot have any loops
The goal is to minimize the number of nodes of the original graph which appear in the "largest" node of the new graph
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines tree decomposition in this passage.

assertions.value: The authors define treewidth as the number of variables in the largest node of the tree decomposition minus one, a convention chosen so that a graph without loops (a tree) has a treewidth of one.
assertions.anchor: Graph theory: treewidth and tree decompositions, paragraph 3
quotes: this property is defined as the number of variables in the largest node of the tree decomposition minus one.
to guarantee that a graph without loops (a tree) will have a treewidth of one.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines treewidth in this passage.

assertions.value: The authors state that it is not possible to map a graph with a given treewidth into a graph with a smaller treewidth, and they offer it as intuitive without proving it in the lesson.
assertions.anchor: Graph theory: treewidth and tree decompositions, paragraph 3
quotes: The key property of treewidth is that it is not possible to map a graph with a given treewidth into a graph with a smaller treewidth, this is hopefully somewhat intuitive.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as a key property with an appeal to intuition and no statement of conditions or proof; the embedding notion it applies to is not defined in the lesson.
assertions.reader_inference: The precise statement (for example, that a graph minor cannot have larger treewidth than the graph it is a minor of) is not given; the claim is stated for 'any' mapping, which the lesson does not define.

assertions.value: The authors state that dynamic programming algorithms can solve certain NP-hard problems efficiently on graphs with low treewidth even with many variables, and that a mapping from high to low treewidth graphs would show P=NP.
assertions.anchor: Graph theory: treewidth and tree decompositions, paragraph 3
quotes: certain dynamical programming algorithms can solve NP-hard problems on graphs with low treewidth efficiently, even if the problem involves a large number of variables.
This implies that if a mapping were possible from high to low treewidth graphs, it would show P=NP.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without citation or proof in the lesson.
assertions.reader_inference: The implication holds only if the mapping is efficient (polynomial time) and preserves the problem; the lesson does not state these conditions.

assertions.value: The authors state that finding the most optimal tree decomposition is in general a computationally hard problem, though in some cases simple arguments about the treewidth are possible.
assertions.anchor: Graph theory: treewidth and tree decompositions, paragraph 3
quotes: In general finding the most optimal tree decomposition is a computationally hard problem, but in some cases it is possible to make simple arguments about the treewidth.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit on its own method in this sentence.

assertions.value: The authors state that the most optimal tree decomposition of a fully connected graph puts every node in the same new node, making its treewidth n-1 for a graph of size n.
quotes: this makes the treewidth of a fully connected graph of size n equal to n-1.
assertions.certainty_reason: The statement is given with a one-line argument, and the conditions of a formal theorem are not quoted.
assertions.reader_inference: This is the standard result that a complete graph on n nodes has treewidth n-1.

assertions.value: The authors say that a highly connected graph should also have a treewidth close to the number of nodes, and that they do not prove it here.
quotes: I won't prove it here, but it should also be intuitively clear that a highly connected graph should also have a treewidth close to the number of nodes.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim the paper states it does not prove.
assertions.reader_inference: 'Highly connected' is not defined, so the claim carries no stated condition.

assertions.value: The authors describe a tree decomposition for a quasi-planar graph that divides it into overlapping rows, each of twice the interaction range and spaced by the interaction range, so that each row overlaps only with the row above and the row below and the resulting graph has no loops.
quotes: we divide the graph into overlapping rows which each have a size of twice the interaction range, and spaced by the interaction range.
Each of these rows will overlap only with the row above it and the row below it so therefore the graph resulting from this decomposition will have no loops.
assertions.certainty_reason: A construction argued in prose, not stated as a theorem with its conditions.

assertions.value: The authors state that for an n-by-n quasi-planar graph, where the interaction range is much smaller than the graph size, the number of nodes in each row is proportional to n while the total number of nodes is proportional to n squared, so the size of highly connected graphs that can be mapped scales as the square root of the size of the hardware interactivity graph.
quotes: For an n-by-n quasi-planar graph (where the interaction range is much smaller than the graph size), the number of nodes in each row is proportional to n but the total number of nodes is proportional to n 2
therefore the size of highly connected graphs which can be mapped scales as the square root of the size of the hardware interactivity graph if it is quasi-planar.
assertions.certainty_reason: An informal scaling argument, not a theorem; it relies on the unproved claim that mapping cannot reduce treewidth.
assertions.reader_inference: The argument gives an upper bound on treewidth of order n from the row decomposition. The conclusion about the largest mappable problem follows only through the no-reduction property of treewidth.

assertions.value: The authors work an example with a quasi-planar graph of n=25 nodes, for which they show the treewidth cannot be more than 9, and they state this implies it is impossible to map a fully connected problem with more than 10 nodes to it by any method.
assertions.anchor: Treewidth of different graphs, final paragraph (figure not in text layer)
quotes: In this example, the graph has n=25 nodes, but we have shown the treewidth cannot be more than 9.
This treewidth implies that it is impossible to map a fully connected problem with more than 10 nodes to it by any method.
assertions.certainty_reason: A worked illustration whose decomposition is in a figure the text layer does not carry; the 'any method' conclusion rests on the unproved no-reduction property.
assertions.reader_inference: A fully connected problem of 10 nodes has treewidth 9, so the bound of 9 is consistent with the stated limit of 10 nodes, given the no-reduction property.

assertions.value: The authors state that a more optimal decomposition of the n=25 example graph is possible and that its treewidth is actually only 6, and they pose as an exercise finding the decomposition whose largest grouping holds only 7.
assertions.anchor: Treewidth of different graphs, final paragraph
quotes: In this example, the graph has n=25 nodes
Note that a more optimal (but more complicated to draw) decomposition is possible, but this simple one demonstrates the necessary scaling. The treewidth of this graph is actually only 6.
Can you figure out the corresponding decomposition with the largest grouping containing only 7?
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without the decomposition or a proof in the text.
assertions.reader_inference: A treewidth of 6 means a largest grouping of 7 nodes, which matches the closing question. The 25-node graph is probably a 5-by-5 grid, whose treewidth is known to be 5, not 6; the lesson does not say which quasi-planar graph it uses, so this cannot be checked from the text.
